native_description_whole: For an arbitrary antimorphic involution theta, a finite word with alternating theta-periods p and q and length at least p+q-gcd(p,q) has alternating theta-period gcd(p,q). This proves the exact unnumbered conjecture after Theorem 23 on printed page 2220 of Nowotka's contribution, joint with Bischoff, to the 2010 Oberwolfach mini-workshop on combinatorics on words. The common finite extension theta(w)w has ordinary periods 2p and 2q; classical Fine-Wilf and central reflection give the alternating conclusion. A reversal example shows that the sufficient formula cannot be reduced by one uniformly; pairwise optimality is not asserted. The research note credits Fine and Wilf, the originating report and Bischoff's thesis, and compares the related Czeizler-Kari-Seki, Kari-Seki and Simpson results. A portable verification supplement preserves the submitted proof, three independent adversarial mathematical audits, complete finite-control outputs and a dated bounded priority audit. No earlier exact theorem was found in the inspected primary sources, without a global novelty or first-discovery certificate; access and version gaps are explicit. AI tools were used extensively in solving, verification, literature research, writing, computation and adversarial review. original_printed_abstract_whole_TeX:
Let $\theta$ be an antimorphic involution of a free monoid. If a finite
word $w$ has alternating $\theta$-periods $p,q$ and
$|w|\ge p+q-\gcd(p,q)$, then $\gcd(p,q)$ is an alternating
$\theta$-period of $w$. This proves the unnumbered conjecture stated
after Theorem 23 in Nowotka's contribution, joint with Bischoff, to
\emph{Mini-Workshop: Combinatorics on Words} (2010). The proof applies
the classical Fine--Wilf theorem to the common reflected extension
$\theta(w)w$ and recovers the alternating phase at its center.
The length formula cannot be decreased by one uniformly.
